item.title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs

version.stem: The graph of f consists of straight line segments connecting (0, 1), (2, 7), (5, 1), and (7, 3), in that order. Which statement correctly describes the graph from x = 2 to x = 5?

choices.rationale: Sign-loss error: using only the magnitude of the slope ignores its direction. The graph falls as x increases on the requested interval, so its average rate of change is negative. Fix: Subtract endpoint outputs in the same order as endpoint inputs.
choices.choice_text: The graph increases with an average rate of change of 2.

choices.rationale: Output-change-only error: −6 is the change in f, not the average rate of change. The input changes by 3, so the slope is −6/3 = −2. Fix: Divide the output change by the input change.
choices.choice_text: The graph decreases with an average rate of change of −6.

choices.rationale: Whole-graph interval error: 2/7 is the average rate of change from x = 0 to x = 7. Those endpoints do not describe the requested interval, where the graph decreases. Fix: Identify the requested interval’s endpoints before computing its secant slope.
choices.choice_text: The graph increases with an average rate of change of 2/7.

choices.rationale: On this interval, the graph falls from 7 to 1 as x increases from 2 to 5. Its average rate of change is (1−7)/(5−2) = −2, matching the downward slope.
choices.choice_text: The graph decreases with an average rate of change of −2.

asset.alt_text: Straight segments connect the points (0,1), (2,7), (5,1) and (7,3), in that order. The x axis runs from 0 to 7; the vertical axis is labeled f(x).
asset.long_description: Straight segments connect the points (0,1), (2,7), (5,1) and (7,3), in that order. The x axis runs from 0 to 7; the vertical axis is labeled f(x).

item.title: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

version.stem: Two bar charts show favorite music genre. For 200 freshmen, the vertical axis is in counts, and the pop bar has height 60. For 50 seniors, the vertical axis is in percent of seniors, and the pop bar has height 40. Which comparison is valid?

choices.rationale: Tempting because the bar heights look comparable — but one axis is counts and the other is percent. Fix: put both on the same scale before comparing heights.
choices.choice_text: A larger share of freshmen prefer pop, because the freshman bar (60) is taller than the senior bar (40).

choices.rationale: Tempting because both bars represent one genre — but the bars measure different things. Fix: compute 60/200 = 30% and compare it with 40%.
choices.choice_text: The same share of each grade prefers pop, because both bars show the pop category.

choices.rationale: This earns the point because the groups have different sizes, so each bar must be converted to the same scale. 60 of 200 freshmen is 30%, which is less than the 40% of seniors.
choices.choice_text: A larger share of seniors than freshmen prefer pop: 40% of seniors versus 30% of freshmen.

choices.rationale: Tempting because unequal group sizes seem to block a fair comparison — but converting counts to percents is exactly how unequal groups are compared. Fix: use relative frequencies.
choices.choice_text: No comparison is possible, because the two grades have different numbers of students.

asset.alt_text: Freshmen panel: n=200, vertical axis Count from 0 to 200, Pop bar height 60. Seniors panel: n=50, vertical axis Percent from 0 to 100, Pop bar height 40. Only the Pop category is displayed; other genres are unspecified.
asset.long_description: Freshmen panel: n=200, vertical axis Count from 0 to 200, Pop bar height 60. Seniors panel: n=50, vertical axis Percent from 0 to 100, Pop bar height 40. Only the Pop category is displayed; other genres are unspecified.

item.title: Tabular and Graphical Representations for the Distributions of Two Categorical Variables

version.stem: A segmented bar chart shows, for each of two clubs, the percent of members who prefer online meetings: 40% of Chess Club members and 75% of Art Club members. Which statement can be made from the chart alone?

choices.rationale: Tempting because 75% looks bigger than 40% — but the chart hides the club sizes, so counts cannot be compared. Fix: compare percents as percents, and find each group's total before you compare counts.
choices.choice_text: More Art Club members than Chess Club members prefer online meetings.

choices.rationale: Tempting because every bar reaches 100% — but each bar is scaled to its own group. Fix: read each bar as 100% of its own group, and look for the group counts before you compare sizes.
choices.choice_text: The two clubs have the same number of members, because each bar is the same total height.

choices.rationale: Tempting because a bigger percentage seems to mean a bigger group — but a percentage tells only what share, not how many. Fix: use a table or side-by-side counts for group sizes.
choices.choice_text: Art Club has more members than Chess Club, because a larger share prefers online meetings.

choices.rationale: This earns the point because a segmented bar chart shows each group's own percentages, so proportions can be compared across groups. 75% is greater than 40%.
choices.choice_text: A greater proportion of Art Club members than Chess Club members prefer online meetings.

asset.alt_text: Both bars total 100 percent of their own club. Chess: online 40 percent, not online 60 percent. Art: online 75 percent, not online 25 percent. Dark segments denote online; light segments denote not online. No membership counts are specified.
asset.long_description: Both bars total 100 percent of their own club. Chess: online 40 percent, not online 60 percent. Art: online 75 percent, not online 25 percent. Dark segments denote online; light segments denote not online. No membership counts are specified.
